title: Worksheet 11: Off-by-One Errors
directions: Read the paragraph below carefully. Then answer all questions using ONLY the information in the paragraph. Circle the letter of the best answer.
paragraph: An off-by-one error is a common programming mistake where a loop repeats one time too many or one time too few, usually caused by a small mistake in how the loop's starting point, ending point, or comparison is written. For example, if a programmer wants to print the numbers 1 through 10, but accidentally writes a loop that stops once a counter reaches 10 using a "less than" comparison instead of a "less than or equal to" comparison, the loop would actually stop after printing only up through 9, missing the number 10 entirely, because the condition "counter is less than 10" becomes false exactly when the counter reaches 10. Off-by-one errors are especially common when working with list indexes, since list indexing typically starts at 0 rather than 1, meaning a list containing exactly 10 items has valid indexes running from 0 to 9, not from 1 to 10; a programmer who forgets this and tries to access index 10 in a 10-item list would encounter an error, since no item actually exists at that position. Careful attention to exactly which values are included or excluded by a loop's condition is one of the most important habits for avoiding off-by-one errors.
